lessons.title: Photosynthesis, Limiting Factors and the Inverse Square Law

before.content_html:
Photosynthesis: The Equation

Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction: it absorbs light energy and stores it as chemical energy in glucose. It takes place in the chloroplasts of plant cells, where the green pigment chlorophyll absorbs light.

The word equation is:

$$\text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} \text{glucose} + \text{oxygen}$$

The balanced symbol equation is:

$$6CO_2 + 6H_2O \xrightarrow{\text{light}} C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2$$

Key Fact

Photosynthesis is endothermic: \(6CO_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2\). It occurs in chloroplasts, uses light energy absorbed by chlorophyll, and produces glucose (for energy and biosynthesis) plus oxygen (released as a by-product).

Plants use photosynthetically produced glucose for multiple purposes: respiration (releasing energy for cell processes); converting to starch for storage in roots and leaves; producing cellulose for cell wall synthesis; combining with mineral ions (especially nitrates from the soil) to make amino acids and then proteins; and producing lipids for storage in seeds and cell membranes.

Leaves are adapted to maximise photosynthesis: a broad, flat surface area captures light; a thin leaf means CO₂ does not have to diffuse far to reach chloroplasts; a network of veins supplies water and removes glucose. The waxy cuticle on the upper surface reflects excess light at very high intensities, preventing photoinhibition of the chloroplast enzymes.

Limiting Factors

A limiting factor is one that, when in short supply, prevents photosynthesis from proceeding faster regardless of how much of the other factors is available. Three main factors limit the rate of photosynthesis:

  • Light intensity — as light increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases (more energy for the light-dependent reactions), until another factor becomes limiting.
  • Carbon dioxide concentration — CO₂ is a raw material; increasing its concentration raises the rate until light or temperature limits it.
  • Temperature — higher temperatures speed up enzyme-controlled reactions in the chloroplast up to an optimum (around 25–35°C for most plants); above the optimum, enzymes denature and the rate falls sharply.

A common exam graph shows rate of photosynthesis on the y-axis against light intensity on the x-axis, at two different CO₂ concentrations. The curve for high CO₂ rises more steeply and reaches a higher plateau. Where the curve flattens, the current factor (light) is no longer limiting — another factor (CO₂ or temperature) has become limiting. Adding more CO₂ shifts the plateau upwards; raising temperature (to a safe level) also lifts the plateau. These graphs test whether you can identify which factor is limiting at each part of the curve.

The Inverse Square Law

Light intensity decreases with distance from the source according to the inverse square law:

$$\text{light intensity} \propto \frac{1}{d^2}$$

where \(d\) is the distance from the light source. This means that if you move a lamp from 10 cm to 20 cm away from a plant — doubling the distance — the light intensity falls to \(\frac{1}{4}\) of its original value (not half). If the distance triples, intensity falls to \(\frac{1}{9}\).

Problem: A lamp is placed 15 cm from pondweed and produces a rate of 20 bubbles per minute. The lamp is moved to 30 cm. Predict the new rate.

Step 1: Distance doubles (15 → 30 cm), so the intensity becomes \(\frac{1}{2^2} = \frac{1}{4}\) of the original.

Step 2: New rate \(= 20 \times \frac{1}{4} = 5\) bubbles per minute.

Note: this assumes light is the only limiting factor. In practice, the curve may already be at a plateau, in which case the prediction would overestimate the change.

Core Practical: Investigating the Effect of Light Intensity on Photosynthesis

The standard method uses aquatic pondweed (such as Elodea) or algae beads. Oxygen produced by photosynthesis is collected as bubbles (or measured as percentage O₂ saturation with a sensor) as a proxy for photosynthesis rate.

Independent variable: Distance of the lamp from the plant (used as a measure of light intensity).

Dependent variable: Number of oxygen bubbles produced per minute (or O₂ sensor reading).

Control variables: CO₂ concentration (maintained by adding sodium hydrogen carbonate solution to the water); temperature (water jacket around the plant, or temperature-controlled water bath); same plant cutting for each measurement.

Key precautions: Allow the plant to equilibrate at each distance for several minutes before counting bubbles. A thermometer measures temperature — it does not control it; the water bath or jacket controls temperature. Repeat each distance at least three times and calculate a mean to reduce the effect of anomalous results.

Analysing results: Plot rate of photosynthesis against distance (or against light intensity calculated using the inverse square law). A curved relationship indicates a limiting factor effect. If plotting rate vs. \(\frac{1}{d^2}\) gives a straight line through the origin, light intensity is the sole limiting factor at those distances.

Key Fact

In the light intensity core practical: the independent variable is lamp distance; the dependent variable is bubble rate. A thermometer measures temperature — a water bath or jacket controls it. Adding sodium hydrogen carbonate to the water controls CO₂ concentration, ensuring light is the only variable changing.

Which of the following is correct about photosynthesis?
A) It is an exothermic reaction that releases energy
B) It takes place in the mitochondria of plant cells
C) It is an endothermic reaction that absorbs light energy
D) It produces carbon dioxide and water as products
practice_questions.marks: C) It is an endothermic reaction that absorbs light energy [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
A student places pondweed at a distance of 10 cm from a lamp and counts 40 bubbles per minute. They then move the lamp to 20 cm.

Using the inverse square law, calculate the predicted rate of photosynthesis at 20 cm. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
• Distance doubles, so intensity = 1 ÷ 2² = 1/4 of original [1 mark]
• New rate = 40 × 1/4 = 10 bubbles per minute [1 mark]
• Units stated correctly (bubbles per minute) [1 mark]
[3 marks] — ECF: if incorrect ratio used but calculation is consistent, award ECF on final answer

practice_questions.text:
A student investigates the effect of CO₂ concentration on the rate of photosynthesis at two light intensities (high and low).

Explain what would happen to the rate of photosynthesis at high light intensity as CO₂ concentration is increased from very low to very high.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At low CO₂, rate is low because CO₂ is the limiting factor; increasing CO₂ increases the rate as more raw material is available; rate continues to rise; eventually light or temperature becomes the new limiting factor; rate plateaus at a level determined by the next limiting factor — student links each change causally.
Secure: Rate increases as CO₂ increases; plateau explained as another factor becoming limiting.
Developing: Rate increases mentioned; plateau stated but reason not explained.
Emerging: Simple statement that more CO₂ means more photosynthesis.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the method a student should use to investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis using pondweed. Include the variables and how to ensure the results are reliable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Independent variable — lamp distance from plant; dependent variable — bubble count per minute (or O₂ sensor reading); controls — temperature (water bath), CO₂ concentration (sodium hydrogen carbonate solution), same plant cutting; equilibrate at each distance before recording; repeat each distance 3+ times and calculate mean; plot rate vs distance or vs 1/d²; thermometer measures temperature — water bath controls it.
Secure: At least four of: IV, DV, two controls, repeats, equilibration, analysis method.
Developing: Basic method described; at least two variables identified; some mention of repeats.
Emerging: Partial method; few control variables; no analysis plan.
[6 marks — level of response]

practice_questions.text: Explain why plants use glucose produced during photosynthesis for more than just respiration.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for any three of:
• Converting glucose to starch for storage in roots and leaves.
• Synthesising cellulose for cell wall construction.
• Combining glucose derivatives with mineral ions (nitrates) to make amino acids and proteins.
• Converting glucose to lipids for storage in seeds or for membranes.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A gardener wants to maximise the growth rate of tomato plants in a greenhouse. Suggest and explain two changes the gardener could make to increase the rate of photosynthesis.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: For each suggestion — one mark for the change, one mark for the mechanism. E.g.: Increase artificial lighting (increase light intensity) → more light energy available to drive photosynthesis beyond the current limiting level. Add CO₂ burners → increased CO₂ concentration means more raw material available for the Calvin cycle. Raise temperature to ~25–30°C → enzyme-controlled reactions proceed faster up to the optimum temperature. Student explains mechanism for each.
Secure: Two valid suggestions with partial mechanism.
Developing: One fully explained suggestion; one partially explained.
Emerging: Suggestions only, no mechanism.
[4 marks — 2 marks per suggestion: 1 for change, 1 for mechanism]

lessons.title: Plant Transport: Xylem, Phloem and Transpiration

before.content_html:
Absorbing Water: The Root Hair Cell

Root hair cells are found on the outer layer of plant roots, just behind the growing tip. Each cell has a long, thin extension — the root hair — that projects into the soil between soil particles. This extension dramatically increases the surface area in contact with soil water.

Water enters root hair cells by osmosis: soil water has a higher water potential than the cell contents, so water moves down the water potential gradient across the partially permeable cell membrane. Mineral ions (such as nitrates and phosphates) enter by active transport, using energy from respiration to move ions from the soil (low concentration) into the cell (higher concentration) — against the concentration gradient.

Key Fact

Water enters root hair cells by osmosis (high to low water potential). Mineral ions enter by active transport, which requires energy from respiration. Root hairs are adapted with a large surface area and thin walls to maximise absorption.

Xylem: Water Transport Upwards

Xylem is a vascular tissue made of dead cells whose end walls have broken down, forming long hollow tubes. The cell walls are reinforced with lignin, which makes the tubes rigid and waterproof so they can withstand the tension created by water moving upward. Xylem transports water and dissolved mineral ions from the roots, up through the stem, and to the leaves — in a continuous column called the transpiration stream.

The water moves because of a continuous pull from above: as water evaporates from the leaves, it creates tension that ‘sucks’ more water up through the xylem. This cohesion–tension mechanism works because water molecules are attracted to each other (cohesion) and to the xylem walls (adhesion), maintaining a continuous unbroken column.

Phloem: Translocation of Sugars

Phloem is a vascular tissue made of living cells arranged in columns. Sieve plates at the end of each cell allow substances to flow between cells. Phloem transports dissolved sugars — mainly sucrose — produced during photosynthesis in the leaves, to all other parts of the plant that need them, including growing roots, developing fruits and storage organs. This transport process is called translocation.

Xylem cells are dead and hollow, with lignified walls; they transport water and minerals upward only (unidirectional). Phloem cells are living, with sieve plates; they transport dissolved sugars in both directions (bidirectional — from source to sink, wherever the plant needs them). Both xylem and phloem run through the vascular bundle in the stem, root and leaf veins.

Transpiration

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plant leaves, mainly through stomata. When stomata are open (to allow CO₂ in for photosynthesis and O₂ out), water vapour diffuses out down its concentration gradient. The evaporation at the leaf surface creates a ‘pull’ that draws water up from the xylem to replace what was lost.

Light intensity: Light causes stomata to open (guard cells become turgid in light). More open stomata = more water vapour lost = higher transpiration rate.

Temperature: Higher temperature gives water molecules more kinetic energy, increasing the rate of evaporation and diffusion from the leaf.

Humidity: In humid air, the concentration gradient of water vapour between the leaf and the air is smaller, so diffusion (and transpiration rate) is lower. In dry air, the gradient is steeper and transpiration is faster.

Air movement (wind): Wind removes humid air from around the leaf, maintaining a steep concentration gradient and increasing the transpiration rate.

Leaf Adaptations for Efficiency

The leaf is adapted to balance photosynthesis and water conservation. A waxy cuticle covers the upper epidermis, reducing evaporation from the flat leaf surface. Stomata (controlled by guard cells) are mostly on the underside of the leaf (lower epidermis), away from direct sunlight, further limiting unnecessary water loss. The spongy mesophyll layer below contains air spaces that allow CO₂ and O₂ to diffuse to and from photosynthesising cells efficiently.

Key Fact

Leaves reduce unnecessary water loss through: (1) the waxy cuticle on the upper surface; (2) stomata mostly on the lower (shaded) surface; (3) guard cells closing stomata in the dark or when water is scarce. These adaptations balance gas exchange for photosynthesis against water conservation.

Calculating Transpiration Rate

A potometer measures water uptake by a plant cutting as a proxy for transpiration rate. Water uptake is recorded as the distance a bubble moves in a capillary tube over a set time. The rate of water uptake (in cm per minute, or cm³ per minute if the bore area is known) is calculated as:

$$\text{rate of water uptake} = \frac{\text{distance moved by bubble (cm)}}{\text{time (min)}}$$

Problem: A student sets up a potometer and records that the air bubble moves 4.5 cm in 3 minutes under normal conditions. Calculate the rate of water uptake.

Step 1: Rate = distance ÷ time = 4.5 ÷ 3 = 1.5 cm per minute.

Step 2: The student then turns a fan on. If the bubble moves 9.0 cm in 3 minutes, rate = 9.0 ÷ 3 = 3.0 cm per minute — the wind has doubled the transpiration rate by maintaining a steeper water-vapour concentration gradient.

Adapting to Extremes: Xerophytes and Hydrophytes

Plants cannot move away from unfavourable conditions — they must be structurally adapted to survive where they grow. Two contrasting environments pose particular challenges: very dry (arid) habitats and waterlogged or aquatic habitats.

Xerophytes are plants of dry environments (deserts, semi-arid grasslands) where water is scarce. Their adaptations focus on reducing transpiration and storing any water that is available. Examples include cacti, marram grass and the Prickly Pear.

Thick, waxy cuticle: A thickened waterproof cuticle on leaf or stem surfaces greatly reduces evaporation.

Reduced or modified leaves: Cacti have leaves reduced to spines, minimising the surface area available for transpiration. The photosynthetic function is taken over by the green stem.

Sunken stomata: Some xerophytes (e.g. marram grass) have stomata sunk into pits or grooves, where air movement is reduced. A layer of humid air builds up around the stomata, reducing the concentration gradient and therefore the rate of water vapour loss.

Rolled leaves: Marram grass rolls its leaves inward when water is scarce, trapping humid air inside and further reducing the humidity gradient.

Water storage tissue: Cacti and succulents have large parenchyma cells in stems or leaves for storing water taken up rapidly after rare rainfall events. Deep or widespread root systems also help collect water from a large soil volume.

Hydrophytes face the opposite challenge: too much water and often too little oxygen in waterlogged soil. They are adapted to float or grow in water and to obtain oxygen for their submerged tissues. Examples include water lilies and pondweed. Hydrophyte adaptations include: large air spaces (aerenchyma) in stems and leaves to transport oxygen from air to submerged roots; broad flat leaves that float on the surface to capture light; and flexible stems that bend rather than break in flowing water.

Key Fact

Xerophytes reduce water loss through: thick waxy cuticles (waterproof barrier); sunken or rolled stomata (trap humid air, reduce concentration gradient); reduced leaf surface area (less surface for transpiration). Hydrophytes are adapted to waterlogged environments with aerenchyma (air spaces) for oxygen transport to submerged roots.

Plant Hormones: An Overview

Plant hormones are chemical messengers that coordinate growth and development. They are produced in small quantities in one region of the plant and transported to where they are needed, where they alter cell behaviour — typically by promoting or inhibiting cell elongation, division or differentiation. The three main plant hormones you need to know are auxins, gibberellins and ethene.

Auxins and Tropisms

Auxins are produced in the growing tips of shoots. They promote cell elongation — cells in the presence of auxin take up more water and grow longer. The unequal distribution of auxins explains two key tropisms:

Phototropism (response to light): when light comes from one side, auxin migrates to the shaded side of the shoot. Higher auxin concentration on the shaded side causes faster elongation there, so the shoot bends towards the light. This positive phototropism maximises the leaf area exposed to light for photosynthesis.

Gravitropism (response to gravity): in roots, auxin accumulates on the lower side due to gravity. However, root cells are more sensitive to auxin — high auxin concentration inhibits elongation in roots. So, the lower side of a horizontal root grows less, causing the root to bend downward (positive gravitropism). Shoots show negative gravitropism — they bend away from gravity.

Commercial uses of auxins: Synthetic auxins (weedkillers) are applied to broad-leaved weeds. At high concentrations, auxins cause uncontrolled, unsustainable growth that kills the plant. Narrow-leaved grass plants are less sensitive to these auxin concentrations, so selective weedkillers kill broad-leaved weeds in lawns without harming the grass. Auxin is also the active ingredient in rooting powder, which stimulates root development when applied to plant cuttings, enabling growers to produce genetically identical plants efficiently.

Gibberellins

Gibberellins are hormones produced throughout the plant that promote growth and development in several ways:

  • Seed germination: Gibberellins break seed dormancy by activating enzymes that digest food stores in the seed (e.g. converting starch to glucose), providing energy and building materials for the germinating embryo.
  • Stem elongation: Gibberellins stimulate internode elongation, promoting taller plants by causing cells in the stem to elongate more than they would otherwise.
  • Fruit development: Applied to grape flowers, gibberellins cause fruits to form without fertilisation (parthenocarpy), producing larger, seedless grapes. This is a major commercial application in viticulture.
Key Fact

Gibberellins have three key roles: breaking seed dormancy by activating food-store enzymes; promoting stem elongation; and stimulating fruit development. Commercially, they are used to produce seedless grapes (parthenocarpy) and to accelerate germination in crops such as barley for brewing.

Ethene

Ethene is unusual among plant hormones because it is a gas. It diffuses through and between plant cells and coordinates several processes:

Fruit ripening: Ethene triggers the breakdown of chlorophyll (causing colour change from green to yellow or red), conversion of starch to sugars (increasing sweetness), and softening of cell walls. This makes fruit more palatable and attractive to seed-dispersing animals.

Commercial fruit ripening: Bananas and other fruits are shipped when unripe (hard and green) to reduce bruising during transport. On arrival, they are exposed to controlled doses of ethene gas in ripening rooms to trigger uniform ripening. This allows supermarkets to sell ripe fruit with minimal waste.

Preventing over-ripening: Conversely, fruits can be stored in low-oxygen, low-ethene atmospheres (controlled atmosphere storage) to delay ripening and extend shelf life. Removing ethene from the storage atmosphere pauses the ripening signal.

Leaf abscission: Ethene also promotes the formation of an abscission layer at the base of leaf stalks, causing leaves to fall in autumn. It coordinates senescence (ageing and breakdown) of plant organs at the end of the growing season.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the role of auxin in phototropism?
A) Auxin moves to the illuminated side of the shoot, inhibiting growth there
B) Auxin moves to the shaded side of the shoot, promoting faster elongation there
C) Auxin is destroyed by light on the shaded side, causing slower growth
D) Auxin is produced equally on both sides regardless of light direction
practice_questions.marks: B) Auxin moves to the shaded side of the shoot, promoting faster elongation there [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain two adaptations of a xerophyte that reduce water loss. For each adaptation, explain the mechanism by which it reduces transpiration.
practice_questions.marks:
For each adaptation (2 marks each):
• Thick, waxy cuticle — impermeable layer on leaf surface prevents direct evaporation of water through the epidermis.
• Sunken stomata — trap a pocket of humid air in the pit; reduces concentration gradient between leaf interior and external air, slowing diffusion of water vapour out.
• Rolled leaves (e.g. marram grass) — leaf curls inward enclosing humid air, reducing the water vapour gradient.
• Reduced/modified leaves (e.g. spines in cacti) — less surface area exposed to air, less evaporation.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A gardener applies rooting powder to the cut end of a plant stem before placing it in soil. Explain how the auxin in rooting powder promotes root formation.
practice_questions.marks:
For each correct point:
• Rooting powder contains auxin(s)/synthetic auxins.
• Auxin promotes cell elongation in root-forming cells at the cut end of the stem.
• This stimulates the formation of adventitious roots, enabling the cutting to develop into a new, independent plant.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Gibberellins are used commercially in the production of seedless grapes.

Describe the role of gibberellins in this process and explain why seedless grapes are commercially valuable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gibberellins applied to grape flowers stimulate fruit development without fertilisation (parthenocarpy); no seeds form because no pollen is required; fruit grows to full size; commercial value — seedless grapes are preferred by consumers (easier to eat); higher yield possible; reduced bitterness from seeds.
Secure: Gibberellins cause fruit formation without fertilisation; no seeds; commercially preferred.
Developing: Gibberellins mentioned; some connection to grape production; mechanism not fully explained.
Emerging: Gibberellins promote growth; no mention of parthenocarpy or commercial benefit.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Ethene gas is used in commercial fruit storage and ripening. Explain how ethene is used both to trigger ripening and to delay it, depending on what is required.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: To trigger ripening — unripe fruit is imported and exposed to controlled doses of ethene in ripening rooms; ethene stimulates chlorophyll breakdown, starch-to-sugar conversion and cell wall softening, producing ripe, sweet, soft fruit. To delay ripening — fruit stored in low-oxygen, low-ethene atmospheres (controlled atmosphere storage); removing ethene from the storage environment prevents the ripening signal, extending shelf life and reducing waste. Student makes explicit distinction between both applications.
Secure: Ripening rooms explained; controlled atmosphere briefly mentioned; both directions of use present.
Developing: One application fully explained; other mentioned.
Emerging: Ethene causes ripening; no explanation of controlled atmosphere or mechanism.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the effects of auxin on shoot cells and root cells, and explain how this accounts for gravitropism in a horizontally placed seedling.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Auxin accumulates on the lower side of both the horizontal shoot and root due to gravity. In the shoot, higher auxin on the lower side promotes faster elongation — the lower side grows longer and the shoot curves upward (negative gravitropism). In the root, cells are more sensitive to auxin — the higher concentration on the lower side inhibits elongation there — the upper side grows faster and the root curves downward (positive gravitropism). Student identifies the key difference in sensitivity (auxin promotes elongation in shoots, inhibits it in roots at the same concentration) and applies it correctly to both organs.
Secure: Correct direction for both root and shoot; differential sensitivity mentioned; mechanism linked to elongation.
Developing: Correct directions stated; one organ explained mechanistically.
Emerging: Shoots grow up and roots grow down; no mechanism.
[6 marks — level of response]

lessons.title: Hormones: Adrenalin, Thyroxine and the Menstrual Cycle

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following correctly describes the role of progesterone in the menstrual cycle?
A) It is produced by the pituitary gland and triggers ovulation
B) It thickens the uterus lining and inhibits FSH and LH
C) It causes follicle maturation in the ovary
D) It stimulates the thyroid gland to produce thyroxine
practice_questions.marks:
B) It thickens the uterus lining and inhibits FSH and LH
[Note: progesterone is produced by the corpus luteum and maintains the lining; oestrogen initially thickens it. However, progesterone also maintains the lining, and option B is the closest correct answer available. Credit B.]
[1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain how adrenalin prepares the body for physical activity during a fight-or-flight response. Give three specific effects.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three effects, each with explanation of mechanism and why it helps: e.g. heart rate increases (more oxygen/glucose delivered per minute to muscles for aerobic respiration); blood glucose rises (liver breaks down glycogen to glucose — more fuel available for muscle contraction); airways dilate (more oxygen can be inhaled per breath — increases oxygen supply to blood). Each linked causally to the survival benefit.
Secure: Three effects named with at least two mechanisms explained.
Developing: Two effects with mechanisms; one is vague.
Emerging: One or two effects named without mechanisms.
[4 marks — 1 mark per explained effect + 1 overall for logical structure]

practice_questions.text: Describe the negative feedback mechanism that controls thyroxine levels in the blood. Name all the hormones and organs involved.
practice_questions.marks:
For each correct point:
• Hypothalamus detects low thyroxine and releases TRH.
• TRH signals pituitary gland to release TSH.
• TSH stimulates thyroid gland to produce and release thyroxine.
• High blood thyroxine inhibits hypothalamus (reducing TRH) and pituitary (reducing TSH), preventing further thyroxine increase.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A student is given a graph showing FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone levels during the 28-day menstrual cycle. The LH surge occurs at day 14.

Explain why the LH surge occurs at around day 14 and what it causes.
practice_questions.marks:

lessons.title: Homeostasis: Thermoregulation, Blood Glucose and Diabetes

before.content_html:
What Is Homeostasis?

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment inside the body. Your cells need precise conditions to carry out chemical reactions — particularly for enzyme activity. If conditions drift too far from the optimum, enzymes stop working efficiently and cells can be damaged or die. The body therefore constantly monitors and adjusts conditions including body temperature, blood glucose concentration, and water balance (osmoregulation).

Key Fact

Homeostasis maintains optimum internal conditions for enzyme activity. All control systems share three components: receptors (detect change), a coordination centre (processes information) and effectors (produce the response).

Most homeostatic systems work through negative feedback. When a variable rises above its set point, the response brings it back down. When it falls below the set point, the response pushes it back up. This keeps internal conditions within a narrow, safe range.

Thermoregulation — Controlling Body Temperature

The core human body temperature is approximately 37°C — the optimum for most enzymes. The hypothalamus acts as the body’s thermostat. It contains thermoreceptors that detect the temperature of the blood flowing through it and compares this to the set point. The hypothalamus also receives information from thermoreceptors in the skin about the external temperature.

The skin is the main organ of thermoregulation. It has two structural layers: the outer epidermis, which is avascular and protective, and the deeper dermis, which contains capillaries, sweat glands and hair follicles. Adjustments in the dermis drive most of the body’s temperature responses.

When body temperature rises above the set point, the hypothalamus coordinates four responses. First, blood vessels in the skin undergo vasodilation — the arterioles supplying skin capillaries widen, bringing more warm blood close to the skin surface so heat radiates outward. Second, sweating increases — sweat glands secrete more sweat, and as water evaporates from the skin surface it absorbs latent heat from the body, cooling it. Third, hair follicle muscles relax so hairs lie flat, reducing the insulating layer of trapped air. Fourth, skeletal muscles reduce any involuntary shivering.

When temperature drops below the set point, the hypothalamus coordinates opposite responses. Arterioles near the skin surface undergo vasoconstriction — they narrow, diverting blood away from the skin so less heat radiates outward. Sweating decreases. Hair erector muscles contract, pulling hairs upright to trap a thicker layer of insulating air. The body also begins shivering — rapid, involuntary contractions of skeletal muscles generate heat through respiration.

Key Fact

Vasodilation widens skin blood vessels, bringing more blood to the surface and increasing heat loss by radiation. Vasoconstriction narrows them, conserving heat. These are both Triple-only topics and are commonly tested in extended-response questions.

Blood Glucose Control

Blood glucose concentration must stay within a narrow range. After eating, it rises; during exercise it can fall. The pancreas continuously monitors blood glucose and secretes two hormones to correct deviations.

When blood glucose rises above the set point, the pancreas secretes insulin. Insulin causes body cells (especially muscle and liver cells) to take up more glucose from the blood. It also stimulates the liver to convert excess glucose into glycogen through glycogenesis. Both actions lower blood glucose back toward the set point.

When blood glucose falls below the set point, the pancreas secretes glucagon. Glucagon triggers glycogenolysis — the conversion of stored glycogen back into glucose, which is released into the blood. This raises blood glucose back to the set point. Together, insulin and glucagon maintain blood glucose in a classic negative feedback loop: each hormone opposes the effect of the other.

Key Fact

Insulin (beta cells) lowers blood glucose: glucose enters cells; liver converts glucose to glycogen. Glucagon (alpha cells) raises blood glucose: liver converts glycogen back to glucose. This is a negative feedback loop. Higher tier only.

Diabetes Mellitus

Diabetes is a condition in which blood glucose is not properly controlled. There are two main types.

Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system destroys the beta cells of the pancreas. Without insulin, blood glucose rises dangerously after meals. It usually develops in childhood or adolescence and is not related to lifestyle. Treatment requires regular insulin injections (or an insulin pump), along with careful monitoring of diet and blood glucose levels. Without treatment, blood glucose can reach dangerously high levels.

Type 2 diabetes develops when body cells become resistant to insulin. The pancreas may still produce insulin but the cells no longer respond effectively. It is strongly associated with being overweight or obese. It is typically managed by dietary changes (reducing sugar and refined carbohydrates), increasing physical activity, and sometimes medication. In some cases, weight loss alone can reverse the condition.

Body mass index (BMI) is calculated as mass (kg) divided by height squared (m2): $$\text{BMI} = \frac{\text{mass (kg)}}{\text{height}^2 \text{ (m}^2\text{)}}$$ A BMI above 30 is classed as obese. Waist-to-hip ratio compares the circumference of the waist to the hips and is an indicator of where fat is stored; higher ratios are associated with greater health risk. Both measures can indicate elevated risk of type 2 diabetes.

before.content_html:
The Urinary System

The urinary system removes metabolic waste from the blood and regulates the water and salt content of the body. It consists of two kidneys, each connected to the bladder by a ureter. Urine passes from the bladder to the outside through the urethra. The kidneys receive blood from the renal arteries and return filtered blood to the circulation via the renal veins.

The most important waste product removed by the kidneys is urea. Urea is produced in the liver when excess amino acids are broken down. It is toxic in high concentrations and must be continuously removed from the blood. The kidneys also remove excess water, excess mineral ions (such as sodium) and other soluble waste products.

Key Fact

The urinary system: kidneys → ureters → bladder → urethra. The kidneys filter urea (produced in the liver from excess amino acids), excess water and mineral ions from the blood to form urine.

The Nephron

Each kidney contains approximately one million tiny tubules called nephrons. The nephron is where filtration and reabsorption take place. Blood enters each nephron’s filtering unit at the glomerulus, which is a knot of capillaries enclosed in a cup-shaped structure called the Bowman’s capsule.

The high blood pressure in the glomerulus forces small molecules out of the blood and into the Bowman’s capsule — this is ultrafiltration. The filtrate contains water, glucose, urea, mineral ions and amino acids. Large molecules such as proteins and blood cells are too big to pass through and remain in the blood.

Selective reabsorption occurs as the filtrate travels along the nephron’s tubule. All glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed into the surrounding capillaries by active transport (which requires energy from respiration). Most water is reabsorbed by osmosis. Useful mineral ions are also reabsorbed. By the time the filtrate reaches the collecting duct, it contains mainly urea, excess water and excess mineral ions — this becomes urine.

The cells lining the nephron tubule have microvilli (tiny projections that increase surface area) and many mitochondria to supply energy for active transport. These adaptations maximise the efficiency of reabsorption.

Key Fact

All glucose is reabsorbed from the filtrate by active transport in the nephron tubule. Healthy urine therefore contains no glucose. The presence of glucose in urine is an indication that blood glucose is too high for full reabsorption — a sign of uncontrolled diabetes.

ADH and the Control of Water Balance

The volume of water reabsorbed by the kidneys is controlled by ADH (anti-diuretic hormone). ADH is produced by the hypothalamus and released by the pituitary gland into the bloodstream.

When the blood becomes too concentrated (e.g. when you are dehydrated or have eaten a salty meal), the hypothalamus detects the low water potential of the blood. More ADH is released into the blood. ADH travels to the collecting duct of the nephron and makes it more permeable to water. More water is reabsorbed by osmosis into the surrounding capillaries, so a smaller volume of more concentrated urine is produced.

When blood water potential is too high (e.g. after drinking a large volume of water), the hypothalamus detects this and less ADH is released. The collecting duct becomes less permeable to water, so less water is reabsorbed. A larger volume of more dilute urine is produced. This is a classic negative feedback loop: the response (changing ADH levels) reverses the original change in blood water potential.

Kidney Failure: Dialysis and Transplants

If the kidneys fail, waste products and excess water accumulate in the blood. Without treatment, this is fatal. There are two main treatments.

Dialysis uses a machine to filter the blood artificially. Blood is passed through a machine where it flows on one side of a partially permeable membrane, while dialysis fluid flows on the other side. Urea and excess mineral ions diffuse across the membrane into the dialysis fluid. The dialysis fluid is carefully formulated to maintain the correct concentrations of glucose and mineral ions, so these are not lost from the blood. Patients typically require dialysis sessions several times per week, each lasting several hours.

A kidney transplant replaces the failed kidney with a healthy donor kidney. If the transplant is successful it gives the patient much greater freedom and quality of life than dialysis. However, the immune system may reject the new organ — to reduce this risk, donors are matched as closely as possible by tissue type and patients take immunosuppressant drugs for life, which increases their vulnerability to infection.

Dialysis is widely available and avoids major surgery, but it is time-consuming, requires repeated sessions, restricts diet and quality of life, and does not cure kidney failure. A kidney transplant restores near-normal function and is a long-term solution, but it requires matching a suitable donor, involves major surgery with associated risks, and requires lifelong immunosuppression. Organ availability is limited by the number of donors.

lessons.title: Exchange, Transport and the Circulatory System

before.content_html:
Surface Area to Volume Ratio

Single-celled organisms can exchange substances directly through their cell membrane because their surface area to volume ratio (SA:V ratio) is large. As organisms grow larger, their volume increases faster than their surface area, and the SA:V ratio falls. A small cube has a higher SA:V ratio than a large cube. For a large, active organism, the surface area of the body wall alone cannot exchange gases or nutrients fast enough — specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems are therefore essential.

Key Fact

As organisms get larger, the surface area to volume ratio decreases. Large organisms need specialised exchange surfaces (e.g. alveoli, villi) and transport systems (e.g. blood) to supply all cells with oxygen and nutrients efficiently.

Alveoli and Gas Exchange

The lungs contain millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli (singular: alveolus). Their structure is adapted to maximise the rate of diffusion:

  • Large surface area — millions of alveoli create an enormous total surface area for exchange.
  • Thin walls — one cell thick, so the diffusion distance is very short.
  • Good blood supply — a dense capillary network maintains a steep concentration gradient.
  • Ventilation — breathing constantly refreshes air in the alveoli, maintaining a high oxygen concentration.

Fick’s law formalises the factors that affect diffusion rate: $$\text{Rate of diffusion} \propto \frac{\text{surface area} \times \text{concentration difference}}{\text{membrane thickness}}$$ This means the rate of diffusion increases when surface area is larger, concentration difference across the membrane is greater, or membrane thickness is smaller. The alveolus maximises all three: large surface area, steep gradient maintained by blood flow and ventilation, and walls only one cell thick.

Blood Components

Blood is a tissue transported around the body through blood vessels. It has four components:

  • Red blood cells — contain haemoglobin, which binds to oxygen in the lungs (forming oxyhaemoglobin) and releases it in body tissues. Their biconcave disc shape increases surface area for gas exchange, and they have no nucleus to carry more haemoglobin.
  • White blood cells — part of the immune system. Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies and provide immunological memory.
  • Platelets — small cell fragments that trigger blood clotting at wound sites, forming a fibrin mesh that seals the injury and prevents blood loss and entry of pathogens.
  • Plasma — the liquid part of blood, which transports dissolved substances including glucose, amino acids, carbon dioxide, urea and hormones.

Blood Vessels

There are three types of blood vessel, each adapted for its function:

  • Arteries — carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. Their walls are thick and muscular with elastic fibres to withstand and smooth out the pressure pulses from the heartbeat.
  • Veins — carry blood towards the heart at lower pressure. Their walls are thinner and they contain valves to prevent backflow.
  • Capillaries — walls are only one cell thick, minimising diffusion distance. They form a dense network reaching every cell, allowing exchange of oxygen, glucose, carbon dioxide and waste with body tissues.
Key Fact

Arteries: high pressure, thick muscular walls, no valves, carry blood away from heart. Veins: low pressure, thin walls, valves prevent backflow, carry blood to heart. Capillaries: one-cell thick walls, site of exchange with tissues.

The Heart and Cardiac Output

The heart is a double pump. The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. It has four chambers: two upper atria that receive blood and two lower ventricles that pump it out. The left ventricle has a much thicker wall than the right because it must generate higher pressure to push blood around the entire body.

The output of the heart is described by the cardiac output equation: $$\text{cardiac output} = \text{stroke volume} \times \text{heart rate}$$ where cardiac output is measured in cm3 per minute, stroke volume is the volume pumped per beat (cm3) and heart rate is the number of beats per minute.

A student’s heart rate is 72 beats per minute and their stroke volume is 70 cm3. Calculate their cardiac output.

Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 70 × 72 = 5040 cm3 per minute (approximately 5 litres per minute). During vigorous exercise, both stroke volume and heart rate increase, so cardiac output can rise to over 20 litres per minute in a trained athlete.

Respiration

Aerobic respiration releases energy from glucose in the presence of oxygen: $$C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O$$ This occurs in the mitochondria and is the main source of energy for all cell processes.

When oxygen is limited (e.g. during intense exercise), cells switch to anaerobic respiration. In human muscle cells, glucose is partially broken down to produce lactate (also called lactic acid). This releases much less energy than aerobic respiration and causes muscle fatigue. After exercise, extra oxygen is needed to break down accumulated lactate — this is the oxygen debt.

In yeast and plant cells, anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide — a process called fermentation. Fermentation is used commercially in baking (CO2 makes bread rise) and in brewing (ethanol is produced).

Levels of Organisation in Ecosystems

Living things exist in a hierarchy of levels. An ecosystem is the largest level: it includes all the organisms in a habitat together with the non-living factors that affect them. Within the ecosystem, a community is made up of all the different species. A population is all the individuals of a single species.

Abiotic factors include light intensity, temperature, moisture level, soil pH, mineral content, wind speed and availability of water. Biotic factors include food availability, predators, pathogens and competition. Interactions between abiotic and biotic factors determine which species can live in a habitat and in what numbers.

Organisms in a community can interact in different ways. Parasitism is where one organism benefits at the direct expense of another (e.g. fleas living on a dog). Mutualism is where both organisms benefit (e.g. oxpecker birds eating insects on cattle — the bird gets food, the cattle lose parasites).

Key Fact

Ecosystem → community (all species) → population (one species). Abiotic factors are non-living; biotic factors are living. Stable communities maintain balanced populations when abiotic and biotic factors are in equilibrium.

Sampling Techniques: Quadrats and Belt Transects

To investigate the distribution and abundance of organisms in a habitat, scientists use systematic sampling methods. A quadrat is a square frame placed at random (using random numbers to generate coordinates) in the habitat. The number or percentage cover of organisms inside is recorded. Multiple quadrats are used to give a representative mean.

A belt transect is used to investigate how species distribution changes along an environmental gradient — for example, from the edge of a woodland into open grassland, or up a rocky shore. Quadrats are placed at regular intervals along the transect line and species recorded at each position. This reveals zonation: changes in species distribution that correlate with the changing abiotic conditions.

Key Fact

Quadrats are used to estimate the abundance or percentage cover of species in a habitat, using random sampling. Belt transects are used when species distribution is expected to change along a gradient. Both are core practical techniques — examiners test apparatus, method, control variables and how data are analysed.

Trophic Levels and Energy Transfer

Energy enters ecosystems through photosynthesis in producers (plants and algae). Energy then passes through organisms at each trophic level as organisms eat each other. At each transfer, most energy is lost as heat from respiration, through waste materials and in parts of organisms that are not eaten. Typically, only about 10% of energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next — this limits food chains to around four or five levels.

Energy transfer efficiency can be calculated: $$\text{efficiency (\%)} = \frac{\text{energy transferred to next level}}{\text{energy available at current level}} \times 100$$ For example, if 10,000 kJ is available at trophic level 1 (producers) and only 1,000 kJ reaches trophic level 2 (primary consumers), the transfer efficiency is 10%. This low efficiency is why fish farming (raising fish in enclosures and controlling feeding) can be more energy-efficient than wild fishing: energy is not lost through the fish swimming large distances or maintaining body temperature in cold water.

Non-indigenous (invasive) species introduced into a new habitat can outcompete native species, leading to population declines or local extinction. For example, grey squirrels introduced to the UK outcompete red squirrels for food and carry a disease (squirrelpox) to which red squirrels have no immunity.

Eutrophication occurs when excess fertiliser (nitrates and phosphates) runs off agricultural land into rivers and lakes. This causes rapid algal growth (an algal bloom), which blocks light from underwater plants, causing them to die. Decomposers break down the dead plant matter, consuming dissolved oxygen. The low oxygen levels kill fish and other aquatic organisms, reducing biodiversity.

Biodiversity and Food Security

Biodiversity refers to the variety of different species in an ecosystem. High biodiversity means ecosystems are more stable and resilient — if one species declines, others can take over some of its roles. Human activities — deforestation, pollution, overexploitation of natural resources — are driving a significant loss of biodiversity worldwide.

Strategies to maintain biodiversity include habitat protection and restoration, reforestation (replanting trees where forests have been cleared), wildlife breeding programmes for endangered species, and seed banks that preserve plant genetic diversity. Maintaining biodiversity also supports food security by preserving the genetic diversity of crop species and the wild species that act as pollinators and pest controllers.

Food security means that people have reliable access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food. Threats include growing global population, changes in climate affecting crop yields, spread of new crop diseases, and limited freshwater supplies. Solutions include developing drought-resistant crop varieties through selective breeding or genetic technology, reducing food waste and improving the efficiency of food production systems.

The Carbon Cycle and the Water Cycle

Carbon is constantly cycled through the environment. Producers remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere through photosynthesis, incorporating it into organic molecules. Animals eat producers and use carbon in their own bodies. When organisms respire, carbon is returned to the atmosphere as CO2. When organisms die, decomposers break down dead organic matter through respiration and decay, releasing CO2 back into the atmosphere. Combustion of fossil fuels is an additional pathway that returns carbon stored over millions of years to the atmosphere in a short time.

The water cycle describes the continuous movement of water between the atmosphere, land and living organisms. Water evaporates from oceans, lakes and soil; plants release water vapour through transpiration. Water vapour rises and condenses to form clouds, then falls as precipitation. Run-off and rivers return water to the sea. Desalination can supplement freshwater supplies in arid regions but requires significant energy input.
before.description: Ecosystems, fieldwork methods, energy transfer, biodiversity threats and the carbon and water cycles.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a community and a population.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: A population is all the organisms of one species living in a habitat at the same time. 1 mark: A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting together in the same habitat.

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would use a quadrat and random sampling to estimate the percentage cover of daisies in a field of 100 m². Include how you would ensure your results were representative.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses random number table or app to generate coordinates; places quadrat at each coordinate; counts number of squares/percentage of quadrat covered by daisies; repeats for a minimum of 10 quadrats (more for reliability); calculates mean percentage cover; control variables include quadrat size, time of sampling; acknowledges any source of sampling bias.
Secure: Method involves random coordinates, multiple quadrats, a measurement of coverage and calculation of a mean.
Developing: Uses quadrats but method for randomisation or mean calculation is incomplete.
Emerging: States use a quadrat with limited method.

practice_questions.text: Explain how eutrophication following fertiliser run-off can reduce the biodiversity of a river ecosystem. Use a chain of events in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Fertiliser (nitrates/phosphates) enters river; algae grow rapidly forming an algal bloom; algae block sunlight reaching underwater plants, which die; decomposers break down dead plants, consuming dissolved oxygen; oxygen levels fall; fish and other aquatic organisms die; biodiversity falls.
Secure: Four of the six steps in the chain, correctly ordered.
Developing: Two or three steps with correct logic but missing key links.
Emerging: States that fertiliser harms the river with one correct point.

practice_questions.text: A food chain in a woodland is: Oak tree → caterpillar → blue tit → sparrowhawk. If the oak trees contain 80,000 kJ of energy, and the transfer efficiency between each trophic level is 10%, calculate how much energy is available to the sparrowhawk.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Energy at caterpillar level = 80,000 × 10/100 = 8,000 kJ. 1 mark: Energy at blue tit level = 8,000 × 10/100 = 800 kJ. 1 mark: Energy at sparrowhawk level = 800 × 10/100 = 80 kJ. Award ECF if one early error is carried through correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the carbon in carbon dioxide in the atmosphere can end up as carbon in the body of a decomposer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A plant removes CO₂ from the atmosphere during photosynthesis and converts it into organic molecules (e.g. glucose, then proteins/fats in the plant body); an animal eats the plant and takes carbon into its own body through digestion and assimilation; the animal dies; a decomposer (bacterium or fungus) feeds on the dead animal by secreting digestive enzymes; carbon is incorporated into the decomposer's body.
Secure: Three of the four steps with correct causal links.
Developing: Two steps, one involving photosynthesis and one involving a consumer or decomposer.
Emerging: States that plants take in CO₂ with little further detail.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of maintaining high biodiversity for the long-term sustainability of ecosystems and human food security.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines biodiversity; explains that high biodiversity increases ecosystem stability (more species to fill roles if one declines); discusses threats (deforestation, pollution, climate change, overexploitation); discusses conservation strategies and their effectiveness (breeding programmes, seed banks, habitat restoration, reforestation); links biodiversity to food security through pollinators, natural pest control, genetic diversity of crops; considers trade-offs (conservation vs. land use for farming); reaches a justified conclusion about the relative importance of biodiversity protection.
Secure: Covers definition, threats, at least two conservation strategies and a clear link to food security, with a conclusion.
Developing: Identifies threats and some conservation strategies but does not integrate food security or lacks conclusion.
Emerging: Gives a general account of biodiversity loss without analysis.
